It is a pleasure to join you today alongside Spain, co-chair of the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, to discuss one of the most urgent challenges of our time, how to accelerate action to fight hunger and poverty as we enter the final four years of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The 2026 State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report shows that hunger indicators have slightly declined for the third consecutive year. This is encouraging, but it is far from enough. In a world capable of producing an unimaginable amount of wealth, hunger and poverty cannot be regarded as inevitable. They are ultimately the result of political choices. Hunger is not simply a matter of food availability. It is, above all, a matter of human rights and political will. Nearly 2 billion people still face moderate or severe food insecurity. Around 2.7 billion people cannot afford a healthy diet. The causes are increasingly interconnected. High food prices, insufficient purchasing power, inefficiencies across food systems, conflicts, climate change, and economic instability. At the same time, the international environment has become more difficult. We face multiple mutually reinforcing crises while international cooperation and developing financing mechanisms are under unprecedented pressure, including a significant decline in official development assistance. We cannot afford to respond to these multiple crises through fragmented approaches. We need to strengthen what has proven effective, mobilize resources more efficiently, and above all, translate political commitments into implementation at country level. This is precisely where the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty has already made a difference. Launched in November 2024, the Alliance represents an innovative approach to international cooperation. Rather than creating new structures or duplicating existing ones, it seeks to connect country-led priorities with proven policy instruments, technical expertise, and financing opportunities. The Global Alliance is now moving from political commitment to implementation. Today, 16 countries are advancing their national plans through the Alliance's implementation process. Recent missions to Ethiopia, Cambodia, and Haiti illustrate this approach. They have enabled the Alliance's support mechanism to work directly with governments, identify priorities and constraints, bring partners together, and explore concrete opportunities for technical and financial support. Ladies and gentlemen, Brazil is proud of the public policies it has developed over many decades in this field. These achievements are rooted in a public policy architecture that combines social protection, school meals, support for family farming, health and nutrition, together with inter-ministerial coordination and institutionalized social participation through the National Council for Food Security and Nutrition. Sharing these experiences is part of Brazil's long tradition in South-South and trilateral cooperation. Through the Global Alliance, we also want to learn from the experiences of other countries and deepen the lessons emerging from implementation. Many of the solutions are already known. We must be ambitious. Four years is a short period of time, but it is enough to make meaningful difference if we act with greater coordination, focus, and urgency. Very much, Mr. Moderator. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I will try to be very brief in the interest of time. Let me start by thanking the co-chairs of the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty for convening this crucial and timely event. Ethiopia, as a member of the Alliance, remains deeply committed to its vision and continues to champion inclusive, climate-smart, locally driven solutions that empower smallholder farmers, promote equity, and accelerate progress towards the SDGs. Our unwavering commitment is also demonstrated by practical application, including through the accelerated implementation of one of our flagship initiatives. As the President of IFAD just mentioned, it's called Yelamat Turrufat, meaning bounty of the basket. So this homegrown program exemplifies Ethiopia's strategic vision food sovereignty, nutrition security, and inclusive economic growth. Launched in November 2022 under the leadership of our Prime Minister, His Excellency Dr. Abiy Ahmed, Yilma Turu Fat has mobilized over 200 districts to boost productivity in dairy, poultry, honey, fish, and meat. In its second phase that lasts for the next four years, the initiative aims to sustainably boost productivity, inclusivity and resilience in Ethiopia's livestock, poultry, agriculture and apiculture sectors by empowering 5 million smallholders farmers with a focus on 65% women and youth. This initiative, which stands out as a first fast track program within the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, have successfully reached the implementation roadmap formulation stage. This milestone signals Ethiopia's full readiness large-scale implementation and reflects program's maturity, the strategic clarity, proven capacity to deliver transformative results in food security, nutrition, and inclusive rural development. GAVI is now well positioned to enter the full phase of implementation, bringing us closer to our shared goals of eradicating hunger, empowering smallholder farmers, and building resilient food systems. We deeply value the all contributions and look forward to our continued collaboration in this transformative journey. The best time is ready to share its experience and collaborate with fellow alliance members to scale up sustainable solutions that eradicate hunger and poverty. We believe that the Yelamathurified model offers a replicable blueprint for fast-tracking food system transformation across the global south. Thank you, Mr. Moderator.

Thank you, Ambassador. Ethiopia is leading the way, not only of the design of the program, but also leading the approach and the way that different actors mobilized each with their different roles in the program. And it's nearing the launch of its implementation roadmap, consolidating all these partnerships. And now I'm very happy to invite another champion of the Alliance, Ms. Dana Boudousea, Vice President for the World Vision International.

Thank you very much. Excellencies, distinguished leaders, colleagues, partners, it's such a privilege to join you, and I want to start by deeply appreciating your leadership in this Global Alliance in a moment when our world needs hope and, equally, practical solutions to close the development gap before 2030. As a Christian relief development and advocacy organization, World Vision is working with some of the world's most vulnerable children, families, and communities, fighting poverty and restoring hope. And for us, fighting child hunger and poverty is foundational. And that's where we are fully aligned with the Alliance's objectives and aspirations. And in too many contexts, we are continuing to see children losing potential when they don't even have access to basic needs. And after decades of progress, we must admit collectively that we are still far from achieving both SDG 1 and SDG 2. We are currently looking at 333 million children who are still living in extreme poverty. And one in five children are living amid conflict, one in five. This climate crisis that we keep hearing about really threatens to affect, to impact the rights, safety, food, healing, and learning all together. But I want to tell you what gives me hope. Because earlier this year in Ethiopia, thank you, Ambassador, for mentioning that, we have seen World Vision colleagues in World Vision Ethiopia sitting at the table, around the table, with Global Alliance partners, including Ministry of Agriculture, FAO, the African Development Bank Group, IFAD, the Brazilian Cooperation Agency, UNIDO, and the World Bank. And what's inspiring is that they were coming together around a shared goal, and that was to identify solutions that can best deliver on the agreed vision, where ending hunger requires collective action. And accelerating action on hunger and poverty creates the space for such important conversations. With only four years remaining until 2030, the challenge is no longer identifying solutions, we know those solutions. The challenge is whether we can scale those solutions and sustain what we already know that it's working. And for me, for us in World Vision, children sit at the center of that challenge. Because when progress stalls for children, the consequences, as quiet as they might be, they are very long-term. And they affect their health, their learning, their economic opportunity, their dignity for years to come. And what today may seem like just a delay, tomorrow it may very easily turn into a lifetime loss of human potential, a lifetime. And three years ago, World Vision launched a global campaign that's called Enough. It was, our campaign is aiming to end child hunger and malnutrition. Today, the campaign is active in 81 countries. And in this three years since it was launched, we have managed to mobilize $3.2 billion in nutrition-related spending. But there is something that qualifies this number that I want to make clear. First, this figure doesn't include the advocacy efforts that were done to mobilize additional funding in public allocations, public funding allocations. And I'm not just talking about national budgets, I'm also talking about local budgets. And I want to give you an example from Bangladesh. Children in Bangladesh mobilized for the budget conversations with their local governments, and the result of that, they were able to convince local government leaders to allocate an additional $311,000 for child-related actions. It doesn't seem like much, but the impact was on reaching almost 400,000 children. This is the power of the civil society to make policy work for citizens, because governments will make changes sustainable when they make their own investment. And the second thing that I want to mention, the figure above doesn't take into consideration the value added by community empowerment and the importance of that community empowerment. And when I was in Ethiopia less than a month ago, what impressed me when I visited World Vision programming in the field was meeting mothers and children, but also community leaders, ambassador, and there is something incredibly inspiring in the mothers who are coming together to address child malnutrition together as a group. And it's in this way in which the practices that you have seen are actually being currently integrated in the national program. And these are practices that are addressing community-based nutrition, livelihood, successes, they are connected with the national plan. And that gives me hope, because we are not reinventing the wheel. We are working with what was documented already. And this is the power of the model that the alliance proposes. I want to close, and in closing, I want to say that we each have very specific things that we can add to the table, and we can each work on our own strengths. And in communities where some of the most vulnerable children live, it takes trust, and it takes persistence and active participation of people themselves so that the solutions that we are proposing can actually be implemented and they can be sustainable. I want to leave you with just one word from Ruth, 16, from Ethiopia. She's the chair of the Children's Council, representing 400 children's local councils. And I asked her what she would like me to bring to this meeting in New York, and she said, "Children need peace." They need access to basic services, including water, food, and education. And in return, we can become a powerful source of progress and hope. But that is currently not happening everywhere. Help us achieve it. Thank you.

Thank you very much for these words and the collaboration of World Vision in the ground in the programs that are developing, as you have rightly pointed out. I wish to invite here the chief economist of FAO, Maximo Torero, to provide this brief overview from the insights from Sophie, and then to be followed, as we are very close and already over time, by the Assistant Executive Director for Partnerships and Innovations of WFP, Rania Dagash, for insights from the Global Report on Food Crisis. So please, Maximo.

Thank you very much, and thank you, Minister Wellington Dias, for being here, and for Spain, for the support of the Global Alliance, as all of you know. And I will be very brief because of the time and I want my colleague of WFP also to be able to speak. The Global Alliance and the support mechanism is hosted in FAO. And what is so innovative of the Global Alliance is the creation of the policy basket, the pillar one, but also the coordination of financing. And I think that's central and implementation at the country level. The Global Alliance is not what FAO does, what others do, or what other institutions does, it's more the coordination and the working together And I think the example of Ethiopia and the example of Haiti too, which is not here today, are two clear examples of how we can change things that are happening and how we can help coordinating not only the best practices that we know, given the numbers of hunger, although they have improved substantially in the last years, we are in 645 million people still in hunger. We need to work together to try to align and minimize the coordination failure that we are facing in the world. Because I don't think it's an issue of lack of money. I think it's an issue of not coordinating the money properly to create investments that are required by countries and that countries are demanding to be able to move out of hunger and poverty. And that's the core, I think, behind the Global Alliance. So again, I am not going to show off all what we do or what other agencies does. I think it's important to put pressure on this coordination so that the investment can have the results that we expect and not only to assume that social protection is a solution because social protection helps, in extreme situations to help people that cannot afford, but we need also to create a transition of graduation of the social protection. And that's where agriculture and what we are doing with Ethiopia and other countries will help us to transform and to really achieve sustainably moving out of hunger and poverty. That's the goal, and that's what we need to aim for. Thank you.
Thank you for these very strategic words and concise on what we need to do and working on that. Please, Rania.

Thank you very much, Renato. Massimo is always strategic, actually, and amazing. Thank you, Brazil and Spain, truly for convening us today. I think exchange is one of the best ways for all of us to learn. So, really, thank you to all of you who shared their experiences today. And it's an honor for me to represent the Global Network Against Food Crises. The message, I think, from the Global Network is pretty clear. Food crises are deepening faster than our collective response. That would be message one. And this is not just about conflicts and climate shocks and economic instability and displacement and disruptions to food and supply chains that are pushing millions deeper into hunger, but it's actually the reinforcement and the interaction between all of those that turns the individual shocks into protracted food crises. And the evidence is rather stark. Over the past decade, Both the number and the share of the people facing acute food insecurity has doubled. The crisis is not receding. The number of people facing catastrophe, or IPC 5 as we know it, has increased more than nine times since 2016. And for the first time in the history of the global report on food crisis, famine was confirmed in two contexts in the same year, parts of Sudan and Gaza. But what's even more important is what the longer-term trends are telling us. 80% of people facing acute food insecurity each year have been concentrated in the same 33 countries. And these 33 countries are facing protracted food crisis, and the majority of them are in all 10 editions of the Global Report in sub-Saharan Africa. This is precisely where prevention and resilience matter most. And while humanitarian assistance to food sectors in crisis context fell by close to 60% between 2022 and 2025, even as the share of the analyzed population facing high levels of acute food insecurity doubled, it brings us to the central challenge. The challenge is no longer understanding the risk, it's acting on it, as many of you have said. It's having increasingly strong evidence about where the food crises are emerging, who is most at risk and what is driving them, and if we can translate that into early, coordinated and sustained action. Every day comes at a cost to livelihoods that are lost, to food systems that are weakened, to humanitarian needs that grow, and the eventual cost of response increases. I'll be quick to say acting early is not more effective, it's more efficient. And ultimately, it's less costly than waiting for a crisis to escalate. But no one can do it alone, and that's why the Global Network Against the Food Crisis is so critical and so unique, because it plays a critical role of bringing us together, builds consensus around evidence and analysis, and collaboration. So what do we need? I'll be very quick. Multi-year financing, sustained investment in social protection, anticipatory action, and shock-responsive systems. Ultimately, we need to build political support, as some of you have said, for a system that acts earlier, but that's about national ownership as well. That way we sustain the gaze longer and we reduce the dependence on humanitarian assistance. And to something new, my sister said, it is central that we urgently restore trust when the international system has credible evidence of an emerging crisis, we translate that into action. Before I hand the microphone to His Excellency Wellington Dias for the closing, I want to end where we started with Brazil. Brazil turned its own experience in overcoming hunger into a global public good. And WFP is proud to carry that experience to countries that need it the most, 15 years later, our center of excellence against hunger in Brasilia remains a powerful example of what is possible when political leadership is matched by partnership, knowledge, and delivery. And we look forward to the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty's two-year anniversary high-level session on the 18th of November, and to working together to turn the four years ahead into measurable progress for SDG 1 and 2. I thank all of you, especially those of you who stayed till this end.

Thank you, Rania. And with these words, Minister Diaz had asked me to close the event very quickly, given we are over time.
